hints: Count the lobes and symmetry in each sketch, a sphere with no directional lobes is different from a two-lobed dumbbell and a four-lobed clover.
walkthrough:
Match shape to orbital type**
Picture what each orbital looks like in 3D. An s orbital is spherical with electron density in all directions, so the solid circle must be s. A p orbital has two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus, like a dumbbell, so the two-lobed shape must be p.

Assign the four-lobed shape**
The shape with four lobes arranged in planes is characteristic of a d orbital. So reading left to right across the table you have p, then s, then d.
Final answer: Left to right: p, s, d.

hints: Recall the Cambridge definition of a transition element in terms of ions, not just the neutral atom, and check the d subshell occupancy in both given configurations.
walkthrough:
Use the correct definition**
A transition element is a d-block element that can form at least one stable ion with a partially filled d subshell. It is not enough to be in the d-block, you must look at the ions.

Check both cadmium ions**
The data shows $[Kr]4d^{10}5s^1$ and $[Kr]4d^{10}$. Both have $4d^{10}$, a completely full d subshell. Because neither ion has $d^1$ to $d^9$, cadmium can never meet the definition, so it is not a transition element.
Final answer: Both Cd ions have a full $4d^{10}$ subshell with no partially filled d subshell, so Cd is not a transition element.

hints: Think of the word roots, mono means one and dentate means tooth, so focus on how many points of attachment the ligand makes to the metal.
walkthrough:
Visualise the ligand binding**
Methylamine, $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$, has one nitrogen atom with one available lone pair. That lone pair is donated into an empty orbital on $\text{Cd}^{2+}$ to make a dative covalent bond.

Link mono to one bond**
Because only one lone pair per ligand molecule is donated, only one coordinate bond is formed per ligand. That is exactly what monodentate means, one tooth gripping the metal at one site.
Final answer: Donates one lone pair to the central metal ion to form one coordinate bond.

hints: Remember an octahedral $\text{ML}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2$ complex can place the two identical $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands either next to each other at 90 degrees or opposite each other at 180 degrees.
Use L for $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$ and draw Cd at the centre with six bonds, showing which ligands are in the plane, wedged out, and dashed back to distinguish the two isomers.
walkthrough:
Set up the octahedral framework**
Put $\text{Cd}$ in the centre with six coordination sites. Label four sites L and two sites $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. In a proper 3D sketch, use solid lines for in-plane bonds, a wedge for coming out toward you, and a dash for going back.

Draw the cis isomer**
Place the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands next to each other, for example one up and one to the right, so the $\text{H}_2\text{O}$-Cd-$\text{H}_2\text{O}$ angle is $90^{\circ}$. Fill the other four positions with L. This is cis-$\text{[CdL}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+}$.

Draw the trans isomer**
Place the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands opposite each other, for example one up and one down, so the $\text{H}_2\text{O}$-Cd-$\text{H}_2\text{O}$ angle is $180^{\circ}$. Fill the other four positions with L. This is trans-$\text{[CdL}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+}$.

Final answer: Two octahedral 3D structures of $\text{[CdL}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+}$ where $\text{L} = \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$:
cis isomer: the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands are adjacent at $90^{\circ}$.
trans isomer: the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands are opposite at $180^{\circ}$.

hints: Think of $K_{stab}$ as an equilibrium constant like $K_c$ but written specifically for the reaction where water ligands are replaced to build the complex ion in solution.
walkthrough:
Connect to equilibrium**
$K_{stab}$ works just like $K_c$. A large value means the complex is very stable and the formation equilibrium lies far to the right. So state it as the equilibrium constant for the reaction that forms the complex ion in aqueous solution.
Final answer: The equilibrium constant for the formation of a complex ion in solution from its constituent ions and ligands.

hints: Use the given $\Delta H_r^{\ominus} = -57$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ for equilibrium 1 to decide whether heating favours the forward or reverse reaction.

Recall that $K_{stab}$ only changes with temperature, not concentration, and link the shift in position of equilibrium to the concentration of $\text{[Cd(CH}_3\text{NH}_2\text{)}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+}$.
walkthrough:
Apply Le Chatelier to temperature**
Equilibrium 1 has $\Delta H_r^{\ominus} = -57$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, so forming the methylamine complex releases heat. If you raise the temperature you add heat, the system opposes this by favouring the endothermic direction, which is the reverse reaction. So equilibrium moves left.

Translate shift into ticks**
Moving left means less product $\text{[Cd(CH}_3\text{NH}_2\text{)}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+}$ at equilibrium, so its concentration decreases. The equilibrium constant for the forward formation, $K_{stab}$, also decreases because the ratio of products to reactants at equilibrium is now smaller.

Final answer: $K_{stab}$: decreases; $\text{[[Cd(CH}_3\text{NH}_2\text{)}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+}]$: decreases.
The forward reaction is exothermic, so increasing temperature moves equilibrium 1 to the left, decreasing $K_{stab}$ and complex concentration.

hints: Compare the two $K_{stab}$ values, $4.0 \times 10^6$ and $4.0 \times 10^{16}$, and remember a larger $K_{stab}$ means the formation equilibrium lies much further to the right.
walkthrough:
Let the numbers decide**
$K_{stab}$ for $\text{[CdEDTA]}^{2-}$ is $4.0 \times 10^{16}$, which is $10^{10}$ times larger than $4.0 \times 10^6$ for the methylamine complex. A much larger $K_{stab}$ means a far more stable complex.

Link to chelate effect**
$\text{EDTA}^{4-}$ is hexadentate and wraps around $\text{Cd}^{2+}$ to form multiple chelate rings, displacing six water molecules and increasing entropy. So when both ligands compete, the EDTA complex dominates.
Final answer: $\text{[CdEDTA]}^{2-}$ is formed in the larger amount because it has the larger $K_{stab}$ ($4.0 \times 10^{16}$).

hints: As a Bronsted-Lowry base methylamine accepts a proton from water, so identify the conjugate acid $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+$ and the $\text{OH}^-$ ion that causes alkalinity.
walkthrough:
Show proton transfer**
A Bronsted-Lowry base is a proton acceptor. The nitrogen lone pair on $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$ takes $\text{H}^+$ from $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, giving $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+$ and leaving $\text{OH}^-$.

Explain alkalinity**
It is the released $\text{OH}^-$ that makes the solution alkaline. Write the equilibrium with reversible arrows as: $$\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+ + \text{OH}^-$$

hints: Identify the reactants, ethanoyl chloride $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$ and methylamine $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$, and recall that acyl chlorides react with amines to give amides plus HCl.
Combine the $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ fragment with $\text{NHCH}_3$ to write the substituted amide product and balance the HCl byproduct.
walkthrough:
Spot the amide link forming**
Ethanoyl chloride provides the $\text{CH}_3\text{C=O}$ group and methylamine provides the nitrogen. The Cl is a superb leaving group, so the N attacks the carbonyl carbon and Cl leaves.

Write the balanced equation**
Join them to make N-methyl ethanamide, $\text{CH}_3\text{CONHCH}_3$, with $\text{HCl}$ as the second product: $$\text{CH}_3\text{COCl} + \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CONHCH}_3 + \text{HCl}$$

hints: Look at the overall change, propanone plus methylamine gives imine P plus water, so focus on what small molecule is lost when the C=O and N-H join.
walkthrough:
Recognise water loss**
The carbonyl $\text{C=O}$ of propanone and $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_3$ combine to give $\text{C=N}$ plus $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Any reaction where two molecules join with loss of a small molecule like water is a condensation.

See the two stages**
Mechanistically the amine first adds to the carbonyl, then water is eliminated to form the $\text{C=N}$ bond of the imine. That is why addition-elimination is also accepted.
Final answer: Condensation (addition-elimination).
